item.title: Riley Gaines says Target Center staffer tried to shut down her Sophie Cunningham sign
item.description: Riley Gaines says an arena staffer told her to lower a sign thanking Sophie Cunningham by name while other fans held signs with player names.
item.content:encoded:
Minnesota Lynx coach Cheryl Reeve was permitted to wear a "Trans kids belong" shirt on the sideline during Sunday’s game against the Indiana Fever.

Fans throughout Target Center held signs supporting their favorite WNBA players.

But when Riley Gaines displayed a small sign reading, "Sophie, thank you — a girl mom," an arena staffer tried to make her put it down.

According to Gaines, the staffer told her the problem was that the sign contained Fever guard Sophie Cunningham’s name.

"I checked all the sign policies before I went in there," Gaines told OutKick. "I made sure it was like 11 by 17. That’s the sign size you could have. So, I got a ruler out. You better believe I was measuring it."

TRANS ACTIVISTS HARASS, HURL SLURS AT SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SUPPORTERS BEFORE FEVER GAME IN MINNESOTA

Gaines attended Sunday’s Fever-Lynx game to support Cunningham, who has faced intense criticism since publicly stating that women’s sports should be reserved for women.

Cunningham was loudly booed throughout Indiana’s 108-100 loss in Minneapolis, while Reeve used the game to make her opposing position clear.

ESPN’s broadcast highlighted Reeve’s shirt and encouraged viewers to listen to the Lynx coach’s previous comments on transgender athletes.

Meanwhile, a staffer inside the arena apparently decided Gaines’ simple message of support for Cunningham needed to disappear.

Gaines arrived at Target Center around 11:40 a.m. local time, approximately 20 minutes before tipoff.

She had initially planned to attend a rally outside the arena but remained at her hotel after her personal security team advised her that the situation had become too hostile.

Gaines was not present for a confrontation outside that was was described by some social media users as an "assault." Video reviewed by OutKick showed one person ripping a T-shirt from another person’s hands, but did not appear to show anyone being struck or injured.

As Gaines entered the arena, however, she said a protester stationed near the entrance put a bullhorn near her face, sounded it and shouted at her.

Once inside, the response was mixed.

Gaines said some people directed insults and hostile looks toward her, but many others requested photographs, thanked her, offered fist bumps and quietly expressed support for her position. She said some people even brought copies of Gaines' book into the arena and asked her to sign them.

Around halftime, Gaines said families and young girls formed something resembling a photo line near her seat.

"There were so many people stopping me, asking me for photos, ‘Thank you for doing what you’re doing,’ winks and whispers and fist bumps, people buying me drinks," Gaines said.

At some point during the game, she held up her sign.

"I see an arena staffer, someone who’s on the court wearing the all-black official clothing, who points at me and mouths something," Gaines recalled. "I can’t hear him because he’s so far away, but he appeared to say, ‘Put your sign down.’"

At first, Gaines wasn’t sure the staffer was addressing her. Numerous other people in the arena were holding signs, including signs containing the names of players.

The staffer eventually approached her and repeated the instruction.

"He comes over and he says, ‘You have to take your sign down.’ I’m like, ‘No, I don’t. I checked all the sign policies before I went in there,’" Gaines said.

Gaines asked why her sign was prohibited.

"He said, ‘Well, because it has her name on it. It has Sophie’s name on it, so you can’t have that,’" Gaines recalled.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM FANS ALLEGE STORM PLAYERS, EXEC HECKLED GIRLS DURING GAME OVER SUPPORT OF WOMEN'S SPORTS

The explanation immediately drew objections from other spectators in Gaines’ section.

"My whole section at that point, they were outraged," Gaines said. "They were like, ‘You can’t tell her she can’t have that. There’s a hundred signs right here with people’s names on it. What do you mean she can’t have it?’"

Gaines refused to lower the sign.

"What are you going to do, kick me out?" Gaines recalled thinking. "Go for it."

She said the staffer eventually returned after the game and apologized. Gaines interpreted the apology as a possible indication that he had been directed by someone else to confront her, though she did not know who may have issued that instruction.

Target Center’s published poster and signage policy does not prohibit signs merely because they contain a player’s name.

The policy states:

"As a general rule, posters/signage under 11 x 17 inches are allowed in Target Center, pending individual tour/promoter approval. All posters/signage must be handheld, may not be mounted on sticks or poles, may not be lit or constructed using lighting elements, may not contain offensive language or graphics and may not prevent other guests from seeing the stage/event."

The venue reserves the right to confiscate signs it considers inappropriate and says the policy may change based on requirements for a particular event. But the policy does not state that a sign is prohibited simply because it includes a player’s name.

Gaines said her sign was handheld, smaller than the maximum dimensions and contained no offensive language or graphics. She also said she made certain it complied with the published size restriction before bringing it to the game.

More importantly, Gaines said the staffer didn't tell her that the sign was oversized, offensive, obstructing another fan’s view or violating an event-specific restriction.

CHERYL REEVE SENDS CLEAR MESSAGE TO SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM WITH ‘TRANS KIDS BELONG’ SHIRT DURING FEVER-LYNX GAME

He allegedly told her she could not display it because it contained Cunningham’s name.

OutKick contacted the Minnesota Lynx and asked whether an event-specific signage policy was in place, why Gaines was instructed to lower her sign, whether any policy prohibited Cunningham’s name and whether the direction originated with the Lynx, Target Center, arena security or the WNBA.

The Lynx did not respond to our email.

Cunningham was booed when she entered the game and frequently when she touched the basketball.

But Gaines said the public hostility didn't match many of the private interactions she had with fans inside Target Center and said she believes many people inside the arena agreed with Cunningham but didn't feel comfortable expressing that support openly.

"I absolutely think she had more fans there, or people who at least support her sentiment, than are willing to admit," Gaines said.

Cunningham eventually made a 3-pointer late in the third quarter and received a noticeable cheer despite playing for the visiting team.

Gaines viewed that reaction as another sign that the loudest people in the arena didn't necessarily represent everyone in attendance.

After the game ended, Cunningham came out to meet Gaines near the tunnel.

Most of the players had already left the court, but Gaines said several young girls remained nearby calling Cunningham’s name.

Cunningham spent approximately 15 minutes with Gaines and posed for a photograph while holding the same sign the arena staffer had attempted to make Gaines lower.

Gaines described Cunningham as completely unshaken by the hostile reception.

According to Gaines, Cunningham said she knew her position was right and remained confident that she could defend it intellectually and morally. Because of that confidence, Cunningham said the reaction did not bother her.

While the loudest voices inside Target Center spent the afternoon condemning Cunningham, young girls waited near the tunnel chanting her name. Fans quietly approached Gaines to thank her. And Cunningham came back out after the loss to greet them.

The arena allowed Reeve to promote her message from the sideline. Fans were free to boo Cunningham every time she touched the ball. But when Gaines held up a small sign thanking Cunningham, a staffer told her it had to come down because it contained the player’s name.

Gaines refused.

By the end of the afternoon, Cunningham was holding the sign herself.

item.title: King Charles makes risky move toward Prince Harry as Prince William 'remains wary': experts
item.description: King Charles reportedly plans to offer Prince Harry a room at Buckingham Palace during his September visit, but experts say Prince William is wary.
item.content:encoded:
Prince Harry's return to the United Kingdom could be King Charles' biggest gamble yet — and Prince William may not like it.

The claim was made by multiple royal experts who spoke to Fox News Digital following reports that the Duke of Sussex is expected to visit the U.K. in September. The Sun reported that the monarch plans to offer his younger son a room at Buckingham Palace in London during his stay.

Fox News Digital reached out to Buckingham Palace and Archewell, which oversees the offices of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, for comment.

KING CHARLES SENDS 'DEFIANCE' MESSAGE TO PRINCE WILLIAM WITH BUCKINGHAM PALACE ROOM OFFER TO HARRY: EXPERT

"Prince Harry has been invited to stay at Buckingham Palace to coincide with the annual WellChild Awards, which he attends each year," British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard told Fox News Digital. "This is perceived as an olive branch by King Charles to slowly rebuild their relationship. However, will Prince Harry accept the invitation? There are murmurs that he has accepted it. Time will tell."

"My sources say staff at Buckingham Palace are against Harry staying," Chard said. "They feel immensely betrayed by Harry's explosive claims against the royal family. Also, my sources say there has been no hint of contrition from the Sussexes. People are not going to forget that they hurled the royal family under the bus, creating lasting damage to the crown. Many wonder why King Charles is appeasing Harry."

The olive branch came after the Sussexes had a rare reunion with Charles during their visit to the U.K. in July. The private meeting, which took place at Charles' country estate, Highgrove House, marked the first time the king had seen his grandchildren, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, since 2022.

WATCH: PRINCE WILLIAM UNLIKELY TO RECONCILE WITH PRINCE HARRY SOON: EXPERT

Harry's recent visit to the U.K. was marked by problems.

After reports that the prince would visit his home country with his family, the British government declined his request for police protection outside royal residences, prompting him to travel alone on July 6.

The Sussexes lost their taxpayer-funded security after they stepped back as senior working royals. Harry was later denied the restoration of that security by the Executive Committee for the Protection of Royalty and Public Figures (RAVEC).

The couple previously lived at Nottingham Cottage on the grounds of Kensington Palace in London before moving to Frogmore Cottage in Windsor shortly before Archie was born in 2019. After they stepped back as working royals in 2020 and relocated to California, the Sussexes were asked to vacate Frogmore Cottage.

People magazine reported that ahead of Harry's trip, his team spent several days exploring ways to make the visit safe through enhanced private security arrangements. Palace sources told the outlet Harry initially declined an invitation to stay at a royal residence before later accepting it.

Harry's spokesperson told the outlet that an offer for the Duke of Sussex to stay at Buckingham Palace during his London visit was withdrawn after he had formally accepted it. Palace sources, however, disputed that account, saying Harry failed to respond by the deadline and that his later acceptance came only after arrangements could no longer be made.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

A source close to the Sussexes told the outlet that, behind the scenes, the drama surrounding the visit was "quite stressful."

"What was billed as a big homecoming ... turned into a nightmare," Russell Myers, author of "William & Catherine," told the outlet. "It was further evidence of the fractiousness of Harry's relationship with the institution."

Katie Nicholl, Vanity Fair's royal correspondent, reported that, according to sources, "not even the Prince and Princess of Wales were made aware" that a meeting would take place on July 10 between the Sussexes and the king.

She also reported that Charles, "who has sworn his youngest son and daughter-in-law to secrecy," insisted that nothing about their July 10 meeting be leaked. Only palace aides were permitted to confirm the reunion had taken place after the Sussexes left Highgrove House without being seen.

Royal experts told Fox News Digital that while Charles is open to reconciling with his younger son and reconnecting with his California-based grandchildren, not everyone is welcoming the Sussexes with open arms. 

Prince William is said to remain wary of his estranged brother, many of them shared. According to the experts, the brothers have not spoken since 2022, when their grandmother, Queen Elizabeth II, died.

"King Charles, from all indications and all feedback from courtiers, obviously wants to maintain an open dialogue and ongoing relationship with his 'dear boy,'" British royals expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital. "Prince William, meanwhile, remains wary and won't want Harry at the palace. However, it's better that Harry stays at Buckingham Palace than in Windsor, which is too close to William and his family."

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

If Charles hopes to bring Harry back into the royal fold, he'll first need the blessing of the future king, royal expert Richard Fitzwilliams said.

"The attitude of the Waleses, since they are the monarchy's future, is pivotal," Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital. "And with good reason, they don't trust the Sussexes. King Charles' approach could prove incendiary."

Still, Chard believes Charles appears willing to risk fresh royal tensions in pursuit of something he's long wanted: reconciliation with Harry.

"Don't get me wrong, reconciliation within the British royal family would be good as it makes the monarchy stronger," Chard said. "However, why invite Harry to Buckingham Palace, the iconic royal residence that's the administrative heart of the monarchy? Harry is no longer a working royal and shouldn't be offered a room at Buckingham Palace."

"I guess the optics of inviting Harry to Buckingham Palace are seen as a goodwill gesture, easing tensions with small steps forward, peace-wise," Chard said. "It also skates over the endless divide within the family."

Chard previously told Fox News Digital that William is known for being stubborn behind palace doors and isn't one to forgive easily.

"William believes the monarchy must be seen to do the right thing, even when it's painful. From what I understand, he felt his father didn't handle that firmly enough. He also believes in protecting it by drawing hard lines. But he's not the king yet."

During part of their U.K. visit, the Sussexes stayed at Althorp, Princess Diana's ancestral home, where they were hosted by Harry's uncle, Earl Charles Spencer. It was there that Archie and Lilibet learned more about their grandmother, who died when Harry was 12, according to People.

Meghan later shared photos of Harry and their children at the estate on Instagram.

Fordwich previously told Fox News Digital that William was likely "livid" over the photos.

"Not only is Prince William likely to be livid regarding the commercialization of Althorp in such a tacky, tasteless media post, but it'll fuel his disgust, so he [would] thwart any major re-entry," she said. "Likewise, Camilla, courtiers, palace aides, security officials and other institutional gatekeepers who are duty-bound to protect the monarchy will all do their utmost to thwart Meghan and Harry's attempts."

item.title: Trump v. Smithsonian: A timeline of how the White House fight over 'woke' history unfolded
item.description: Trump's executive orders target the Smithsonian Institution, arguing exhibits prioritize decolonization and DEI over patriotic American history.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump's effort to root out what his administration calls "woke" ideology at the Smithsonian has grown into one of the most extensive White House reviews of the institution in decades.

The Smithsonian oversees 21 museums, the National Zoo and nearly 157 million objects and specimens while receiving more than $1 billion annually in federal funding outside of private-side dollars.

The administration's campaign has placed the taxpayer-supported institution at the center of a broader debate over patriotism, historical interpretation and the role of federally funded cultural institutions amid a growing divide over how people view and retell America's story.

GOP LAWMAKER DEMANDS ANSWERS AFTER SMITHSONIAN CHIEF URGED MOVING BEYOND 'AMERICA FIRST MENTALITY'

Over the past 16 months, the administration has examined museum exhibits, educational programming, internal records and leadership statements, issued multiple document requests, interviewed curators and conducted on-site museum walkthroughs.

The effort culminated in a 162-page White House report recommending sweeping reforms and announcing new executive actions aimed at implementing those recommendations.

Here's a timeline of the major developments.

Trump signed an executive order titled "Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History" two months into his second term. The order argues that federal cultural institutions, including the Smithsonian, have promoted "divisive" ideological narratives.

The executive action directs the Trump administration to restore what it describes as a more patriotic presentation of American history. And it tasks the White House Domestic Policy Council and Vice President JD Vance, in his role as a Smithsonian Regent, with reviewing Smithsonian exhibits and programs.

Following Trump's executive order, the White House Domestic Policy Council kicked-off an investigation of the Smithsonian, focusing primarily on the National Museum of American History.

Officials reviewed exhibits, educational materials, strategic plans, leadership speeches, museum programming and public statements. During that review, the council documented examples they argue prioritize divisive ideological narratives over a so-called patriotic telling of American history.

White House officials sent Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch a letter formally launching the review ordered by Trump.

The letter directs the institution to turn over exhibition plans, educational materials, internal policies and other records while outlining a review of eight Smithsonian museums to ensure exhibits "celebrate American exceptionalism" and remove what the administration calls divisive narratives.

It also sets deadlines for document production, curator interviews and on-site reviews, with museums instructed to begin revising public-facing content within 120 days.

The White House criticizes the museum for holding no special Independence Day programming in 2025 despite being open on July 4, discontinuing its traditional Flag Day ceremonies, and planning 250th anniversary exhibits and events.

According to the administration, those 250 installations emphasize flaws of the United States while giving insufficient attention to the Founders, the Declaration of Independence and the American Revolution.

The White House tells Smithsonian Secretary Bunch in a letter that the institution has failed to provide most of the records requested during its review.

Among other things, the review requested exhibition plans, curatorial documents and governance materials be turned over.

At this time, the administration gives the Smithsonian until Jan. 13, 2026, to produce the requested records. It also reminds the institution that federal funding must be used in a manner consistent with Trump's "Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History" executive order.

White House investigators complete on-site walkthroughs of Smithsonian museums. During the visits, they reviewed exhibits, educational materials, digital content and internal planning documents as well as interviewed museum staff as part of the administration's review.

SMITHSONIAN'S NATIONAL MUSEUM OF AMERICAN HISTORY PROMOTES 'EXTREME POLITICAL ACTIVISM,' WH REPORT ALLEGES

Investigators found during those visits exhibits that they argue emphasized restorative history, decolonization, immigration activism, DEI initiatives and social justice. Meanwhile, it claimed that the institution was downplaying America's Founders, the nation's achievements and patriotic themes.

The report ultimately concludes the Smithsonian project has undergone a significant shift away from its original mission, arguing exhibits increasingly emphasize social justice activism and ideological narratives rather than focus on America's founding principles and national achievements.

The museum debuts its signature exhibition commemorating America's 250th anniversary, featuring 250 objects from its collection, including Thomas Jefferson's writing desk, George Washington's uniform and the Star-Spangled Banner.

The White House said just two months before the country's 250th celebration that the exhibition repackages existing displays rather than creating a new founding-era exhibit. It also criticized the installation for failing to meaningfully celebrate America's Founders, the Declaration of Independence or the American Revolution during the nation's 250th birthday.

The Trump administration also said the exhibit's promotional materials and programming downplayed patriotic themes and national symbols.

The White House Domestic Policy Council releases its 162-page "Saving America's Story" report, concluding that the National Museum of American History has undergone "ideological capture."

The report recommends removing what it describes as political activism from museum exhibits and restoring displays that emphasize America's founding principles, national achievements and patriotic history. It says the findings stem from the Smithsonian review ordered by Trump's March 2025 executive order.

The expansive report included images of exhibits, images of exhibits and placards, as well as curators and leaders of the museum.

It spent much of the report focusing on how the museum classified and portrayed illegal migration in its exhibits.

Hours after the report's release, Trump signs the "Restoring Trust in the Smithsonian Institution" executive order, directing the Interior Department, Office of Management and Budget (OMB), General Services Administrator (GSA) and the White House Domestic Policy Council to use available authorities to encourage the Smithsonian to address the report's findings.

TRUMP ORDERS SIGNS OUTSIDE SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM AMID ROW OVER ITS DEPICTION OF AMERICAN HISTORY

Trump's order also instructs the National Park Service (NPS) to install temporary signs outside the National Museum of American History directing visitors to the report and describing the administration's concerns with the museum's presentation of American history.

The administration says its effort is intended to restore a more patriotic presentation of American history at the Smithsonian. The institution, meanwhile, has long said its mission is to preserve and present the nation's history through scholarship, research and public education, setting the stage for continued debate over how America's story should be told.

The Smithsonian did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

item.title: First showdown in race for Lindsey Graham's Senate seat puts GOP hopefuls to the test
item.description: Darline Graham, Ralph Norman, Russell Fry and Mark Sanford share the debate stage Monday in the South Carolina Senate race for the vacant seat.
item.content:encoded:
Candidates eyeing the late Sen. Lindsey Graham’s seat of power in the Senate will get a chance to define themselves on the debate stage Monday.

Untested fresh blood, lawmakers eager to ascend and candidates who have failed to launch are set to share the same stage and will get an equal opportunity to convince South Carolinians that they have what it takes to take over for Graham.

While nearly 10 candidates have jumped into the race for the suddenly vacant seat, politicos in South Carolina contend that only a few are true contenders and have the most to prove during the televised sales pitch to voters as campaign materials darken voters' doorsteps.

TRUMP ENDORSEMENT FAILS TO CLEAR GOP FIELD AS FORMER GOVERNOR JOINS SOUTH CAROLINA SENATE RACE

"This debate is the opportunity for South Carolinians to have a moment to hear from these candidates directly," Dave Wilson, a South Carolina-based political consultant, told Fox News Digital.

"The mail is already coming in," he continued. "The emails are already going out, but this is a time to see whether the candidates can handle the job in what is in essence the only job interview that we will see ahead of the primary."

The key candidates to watch are Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., who was appointed to take her brother’s seat and has since received President Donald Trump’s endorsement. Behind her are Reps. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., and Russell Fry, R-S.C., and former Gov. Mark Sanford.

MACE SNUBS TRUMP'S PREFERRED SENATE CANDIDATE, BACKS RALPH NORMAN INSTEAD

And that same group, along with Graham's former primary opponent Mark Lynch, have all qualified for the debate stage under the South Carolina GOP's criteria. 

Wilson contended that both Norman and Sanford have statewide name recognition — Norman unsuccessfully ran for the GOP nomination for governor this year and Sanford has been a known entity in South Carolina politics for nearly two decades.

Graham could ride on the wave of her brother’s last name, but she doesn’t have the record to push like the others in the race. While she’ll be making a pitch about who she is, Fry could stand to gain the most among the other competitors.

TRUMP PUSHES LINDSEY GRAHAM'S SISTER TO RUN FOR US SENATE AFTER SHE GETS APPOINTMENT TO FINISH OUT TERM

That’s because, unlike Norman, Sanford and Graham, he doesn’t have the same statewide campaign infrastructure and name recognition, despite being handpicked by Trump to run for Congress years ago.

"I think Russell Fry needs this debate more than any other person on that stage right now because, while he has been a staunch Trump supporter, he is the one person who could benefit the most from a really strong debate performance," Wilson said. "Because he has to do what it takes to establish himself statewide and demonstrate that what he’s done for the 7th Congressional District, he can do for the entire state."

item.title: Lindsay Clancy jurors visit crime scene in Karen Read-style move to test timeline: Retired judge
item.description: Jurors retraced Patrick Clancy's route to CVS and walked through the Duxbury home where three children were killed during a 40-minute court visit.
item.content:encoded:
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, contact the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

Jurors in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial retraced her ex-husband’s route Friday before walking through the Massachusetts home where the couple’s three children were killed, a court-supervised visit a retired Massachusetts judge said could help the panel understand the timeline and setting at the center of the case.

The move was reminiscent of another high-profile Massachusetts murder trial that recently captured headlines, when Karen Read was acquitted of the top charge during her 2025 retrial.

In Clancy's case, the 18-member jury panel was driven past ThreeV restaurant in Plymouth and the CVS pharmacy in Kingston that Patrick Clancy visited on Jan. 24, 2023. Jurors were then escorted in groups of six through the family’s former home in Duxbury during a roughly 40-minute visit.

LINDSAY CLANCY’S EX-HUSBAND DETAILS ‘BIG SPIRAL’ AS EXPERT SAYS ONE PART ‘SCARED ME’ IN MOM’S MURDER TRIAL

They also saw the basement where Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, were found, as well as the yard beneath the second-story window where Lindsay Clancy was discovered seriously injured after attempting suicide. The fall left the woman paralyzed and in a wheelchair.

Jack Lu, who served 16 years as a Massachusetts Superior Court judge and five years as a Boston Municipal Court judge, said that, in his experience, a view is expected in a Massachusetts homicide trial, particularly a case involving multiple deaths.

"The reality is, on a homicide case, they’re always, always going to do a view," Lu, now a Boston College law professor, told Fox News Digital.

LINDSAY CLANCY’S EX-HUSBAND DETAILS PILL USE AS EXPERT SAYS EVIDENCE COULD SHAPE MURDER TRIAL

Lu said the clearest benefit may be helping jurors assess how long Patrick was away from the home and understand the locations discussed throughout testimony.

"They’re going to dissect the amount of time involved in the husband’s trip to CVS," Lu said, adding that the visit could help jurors understand "what kind of time that Ms. Clancy had" after Patrick left.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Still, Lu cautioned against assuming the view necessarily favored either side or would become decisive.

KAREN READ SAYS SHE GETS FREE MEALS AND DISCOUNTS EVERYWHERE AFTER NOT GUILTY VERDICT

"The view is perhaps not obviously crucial to this case," he said. "It gives them context."

WATCH: Jurors retrace Patrick Clancy’s errands before finding slain children

A similar procedure was used during Read’s 2025 retrial in Massachusetts, where she was charged with killing her boyfriend, Boston police officer John O'Keefe.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Jurors were bussed to 34 Fairview Road in Canton, where O’Keefe was found, and viewed the property and Read’s Lexus. Prosecutors and defense attorneys directed jurors’ attention to different details from the case.

WATCH: Jurors in Karen Read's trial visit scene of John O'Keefe's death

In Clancy's case, prosecutors allege she intentionally sent Patrick on the errands to get him out of the house before strangling the children.

SEND US A TIP

Her attorneys do not dispute that she killed her children but argue she lacked criminal responsibility because she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis.

After returning to Plymouth Superior Court on Friday, jurors heard emotional testimony from emergency room doctors who treated Dawson and Callan.

GOT A TIP?

Dr. Mark Tenerowicz testified that hospital staff tried for about 40 minutes to revive Dawson, who arrived without a pulse and was not breathing. He was pronounced dead at about 7:28 p.m.

Dr. Benjamin Kaufman said medical workers restored Callan’s pulse, but the infant remained unable to breathe independently.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"At no point did he exhibit any brain function," Kaufman testified.

During testimony, Clancy covered her face and appeared to sob and shake during the doctors’ testimony. Lu described the emotional weight of the proceedings as "exceptional," even among heavily publicized trials.

"Even among high-profile cases, the emotionalism of this case is extraordinary," he said, adding that Massachusetts judges are trained to privately address jurors after a verdict about processing the emotional toll of what they went through.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Judge William Sullivan dismissed the panel on Friday afternoon, saying the trial was "well on schedule, if not ahead." Testimony is scheduled to resume Monday at 9 a.m.

item.title: What to order instead: Lettuce-free meals at McDonald's, Burger King, Chick-fil-A, Taco Bell and more
item.description: McDonald's Filet-O-Fish, Wendy's Baconator and Taco Bell's Mexican Pizza are among lettuce-free fast-food options amid the cyclospora outbreak.
item.content:encoded:
As the restaurant industry navigates the ongoing fallout from the cyclospora outbreak, many menu items at fast-food chains don't contain shredded lettuce — the ingredient the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has linked to the outbreak.

Cyclospora is a microscopic parasite known to cause cyclosporiasis, the most common symptom of which is diarrhea. The FDA said it traced the outbreak to shredded iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico.

A McDonald's standard hamburger does not contain lettuce, though the Big Mac, McChicken and deluxe burgers do.

IS LETTUCE STILL SAFE TO EAT AMID TACO BELL ILLNESS PROBE? DOCTORS ANSWER

The standard hamburger contains a beef patty, ketchup, mustard, chopped onions and dill pickle slices on a bun.

Other McDonald's items that don't contain lettuce include the Filet-O-Fish, a breaded and fried fish filet served with tartar sauce and a slice of American cheese on a bun.

The Double Cheeseburger, Quarter Pounder with Cheese and Chicken McNuggets are other lettuce-free options.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Only a few menu items at KFC contain lettuce. They include the chicken wrap and the chain's chicken sandwiches.

KFC's signature items, including the original recipe for fried chicken, chicken tenders, nuggets and the Famous Bowl (mashed potatoes, corn, chicken, cheese and gravy), are lettuce-free.

Several items on Chick-fil-A's menu lack lettuce. The chain's signature chicken sandwich only contains a pickle, as does the spicy version.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Chick-fil-A Nuggets, which can be ordered fried or grilled, as well as the Chick-n-Strips and Chicken Biscuits, are also all lettuce-free.

Though many burgers include lettuce at Wendy's, items that don't come with them include the Baconator, Son of Baconator and the chain's chili.

The Baconator is made with two beef patties, six strips of bacon, two slices of American cheese, ketchup and mayonnaise on a toasted bun. The Son of Baconator is a smaller version of the signature burger and contains four pieces of bacon.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

At Burger King, many of the burgers and sandwiches include lettuce, but the nuggets, Chicken Fries and Rodeo Burger come without it. Chicken Fries are breaded and fried chicken strips in the shape of a french fry. The Rodeo Burger is a beef patty on a bun topped with onion rings and barbecue sauce.

Taco Bell has been offering limited-time promotions on items that do not contain shredded lettuce, including the Mexican Pizza, the Enchirito and regular Nacho Fries.

An Enchirito is made with a warm flour tortilla filled with seasoned beef, refried beans and diced onions and is smothered in red sauce and melted shredded cheddar cheese.

Other lettuce-free options at Taco Bell include the Bean Burrito, Beefy 5-Layer Burrito, Cheesy Roll Up, Cheesy Bean and Rice Burrito and the Quesadilla (cheese, chicken and steak).

Fox News Digital reached out to Chick-fil-A, Burger King, KFC, McDonald's, Taco Bell and Wendy's for comment.

item.title: JASON CHAFFETZ: Democrats desperately need Nancy Pelosi to take charge
item.description: With Nancy Pelosi retiring and DNC fundraising anemic, the Democratic Socialists of America's radical platform forces uncomfortable choices.

item.title: Our enemies found a weakness in essential technology. We must fix it … fast
item.description: Iran's Strait of Hormuz jamming exposed GPS vulnerability as over 1,100 vessels recorded interference in a single day, threatening critical infrastructure.
item.content:encoded:
In July, Iran attempted to make good on its threat to close the Strait of Hormuz. Yet the strait had already ceased functioning as reliable commercial infrastructure long before. Since the conflict started, more than 1,100 vessels recorded GPS and AIS interference in a single day, ships appeared on tracking systems at airports or deep inside Iranian territory, and ship crews navigated one of the world’s busiest waterways by radar alone because satellite navigation could no longer be trusted. Iran did more than threaten a choke point. It demonstrated what a determined adversary can do to the satellite infrastructure the modern world has taken for granted.

America depends on a second, invisible choke point: the Global Positioning System. GPS timestamps every credit card swipe and equity trade, synchronizes the power grid and cellular networks, and guides combines through fields, container ships into port and infantry through contested terrain.

That faint signal – engineered in the 1970s in a different time when our enemies weren't as savvy – now carries the weight of the entire global economy and our military edge. That world is gone. Global aviation logged roughly 430,000 jamming and spoofing incidents in 2024, a sharp 62% increase in a single year. A basic jammer can be built from off-the-shelf parts for a few hundred dollars.

GEN. JACK KEANE WARNS AGAINST TRUSTING IRAN ON STRAIT OF HORMUZ

I know what reliable navigation means in combat. As a Ranger, I never thought about GPS in combat. It located my team, guided the aircraft above us, and synchronized fires without ever announcing itself. We took it for granted. Today’s service members enjoy no such luxury. We are sending American forces into contested spaces with a vulnerable system designed half a century ago.

No incremental upgrade can fix GPS. Its weakness is physics, not engineering oversight. A satellite in medium Earth orbit broadcasting at limited power will always produce a faint signal at the receiver. A nearby jammer will always overpower it. Military M-Code offers marginal improvements but does not change the fundamental math.

China has drawn the obvious conclusion. The Chinese Communist Party is rapidly expanding next-generation navigation satellites, including low Earth orbit (LEO) constellations that operate closer to Earth, broadcast far stronger signals and are designed with electronic warfare in mind.

Beijing aims to dominate the navigation layer of the 21st-century economy. Congress has noted this shift in unusually blunt terms, stating in last year’s defense authorization that the United States is falling behind China in satellite navigation.

The solution is not another slow government program. It is emerging from American commercial industry. U.S. companies have designed and launched navigation satellites in domestic factories using private capital. These systems now operate in LEO, delivering signals up to 100 times stronger than GPS.

They resist spoofing by design, provide centimeter-level accuracy, and work with the GPS receivers already installed in millions of aircraft, vehicles, vessels and weapons. A software update is often all it takes to transition equipment America already owns to navigation that can survive attacks.

The Space Force understands this. Earlier this year, it canceled plans for a government-owned "Resilient GPS (R-GPS)" constellation in favor of leveraging commercial services. The fiscal year 2027 defense bill now advancing in the House would require the Air Force to demonstrate capabilities with commercial LEO providers – testing operation without GPS, resistance to jamming and spoofing, and rapid restoration if satellites are lost.

The demonstration is a good start, but it is not enough. Three concrete steps would turn congressional direction into deployed capability: first, fund what Congress has already directed. The 2027 defense appropriations bill should create a dedicated budget line for the commercial LEO demonstration and follow-on services. This investment would cost a fraction of a single GPS III satellite – and far less than the $1 billion once earmarked for R-GPS.

Second, procure operational services, not more studies. Commercial providers are already placing production satellites into orbit with private capital. The Department of Defense should contract for resilient navigation as a service – just as it does for launch services – and pay for proven performance in orbit.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Third, set resilience standards for critical infrastructure. Merchant crews navigating the Strait of Hormuz by radar this spring used receivers roughly 15 years out of date. Farmers, utility operators, and airline pilots face the same exposure. Federal regulators should establish minimum resilience requirements that legacy GPS can no longer meet on its own.

In 1973, the United States wagered that a constellation of navigation satellites would transform warfare and the global economy. That wager succeeded beyond any planner’s dreams, and it taught our adversaries precisely what to hold at risk. Iran disrupted a strait the world assumed would remain open. Our more capable adversaries intend to disrupt a signal America assumes will always be overhead.

The next era of navigation will belong to the first nation to focus on fielding resilient capabilities. American industry has already placed them in orbit. Whether the U.S. government moves at the speed of relevance will determine if America retains the decisive advantage it has held for 50 years – or cedes it to another power.

item.title: Trump is winning every battle in Iran—and risking the war that matters
item.description: Trump faces a credibility test as Iran absorbs U.S. strikes while China, Russia, and allies assess America's strategic limits and endurance.
item.content:encoded:
Five months into the Iran war, America is winning almost every battle. The harder question is whether we are winning the war.

No one should minimize what the U.S. military has accomplished. American air and naval power have inflicted extraordinary damage on Iran's military infrastructure. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has lost command centers, missile launchers, drone facilities, air defenses, coastal installations, logistics hubs, and key personnel. Our servicemen and women have once again demonstrated unmatched professionalism, precision, and courage.

Those are genuine tactical successes.

I'VE STUDIED MILITARY STRATEGY. TRUMP NOW FACES IRAN'S OLDEST BATTLEFIELD TRICK

But military history teaches a hard lesson: tactical success does not necessarily produce strategic success.

That distinction matters because the strategic center of gravity in this conflict is shifting. In the opening weeks, the focus was rightly on degrading Iran's military and nuclear capabilities. Today, the consequences increasingly extend beyond the battlefield to American credibility at home and abroad.

Iran has shown greater resilience than many anticipated, dispersing forces, hardening underground facilities, shifting to mobile launchers, and continuing to launch missiles and drones despite sustained bombing. Determined adversaries often adapt faster than expected when fighting for regime survival.

IRAN REGIME CHANGE TALK RESURFACES AS TRUMP SAYS TEHRAN 'WANTS TO MEET' AMID US STRIKES

Washington’s campaign appears to assume that destroying Iran’s senior leadership could cause the system to collapse. But the regime’s real source of endurance may run deeper, rooted in a revolutionary Islamist ideology reinforced by the clerical establishment, the IRGC, security organs, patronage networks, and a culture of martyrdom. Leaders can be killed and command posts destroyed, but bombs cannot extinguish an ideology that treats suffering as validation. This doesn't mean American intelligence failed. It may mean Washington's theory of victory placed too much faith in decapitation and physical destruction, when ideologically committed regimes often absorb punishment that planners assume will compel surrender. The real question is whether repeated battlefield success is producing the political outcomes Washington seeks.

That answer is becoming less clear.

Each day brings another successful strike, another destroyed missile site, another IRGC facility reduced to rubble. Yet Iran keeps fighting. The danger isn't that America cannot destroy targets. It is appearing trapped in a cycle of retaliation without a defined political end state.

TRUMP REVEALS THE LINE IRAN HAS TO CROSS FOR US TO RESTART OFFENSIVE MILITARY CAMPAIGN

For President Trump, converting military success into political results is now the central challenge.

Like it or not, President Trump's credibility, and increasingly America's credibility, is becoming the strategic center of gravity. Every warning, every red line, every promise of retaliation is now evaluated not only by Tehran but also by Beijing, Moscow, Pyongyang, Jerusalem, Riyadh, Brussels, and voters here at home.

Credibility is one of America's most valuable strategic assets. It is earned when military action consistently advances defined political objectives. It is weakened when adversaries conclude they can absorb punishment while waiting for Washington's patience, or its public support, to erode.

That domestic support deserves careful attention.

An AP-NORC survey found that roughly two-thirds of Americans believe the war has not been worth fighting, while only about one-third believe it has. Support has softened even among Republicans. Americans increasingly doubt the campaign has a clear destination and worry about its duration, cost, and expansion.

In a democracy, that matters.

Public opinion should never dictate military strategy, but neither can elected leaders indefinitely sustain a costly conflict if Americans lose confidence in its objectives. If these trends continue, Iran could become a consequential midterm issue, especially if voters link it to rising energy costs, strained resources, or distraction from border security, inflation, and China.

America's allies are watching just as closely.

Israel focuses on immediate security. Gulf Arab partners want energy infrastructure and Hormuz navigation protected. NATO allies want assurance that Washington can manage multiple crises without weakening deterrence elsewhere. Indo-Pacific allies are asking whether a war consuming American attention and resources changes Washington's long-term commitment to Asia.

That same question is being studied most carefully in Beijing.

China is analyzing American logistics, missile defense, intelligence, precision strike capability, naval operations, industrial capacity, public opinion, and political endurance, watching how quickly the United States replenishes munitions and how democratic governments sustain support during prolonged conflict.

China is learning about America's strengths.

It is also searching for America's limits.

Beijing may conclude that America can destroy fixed targets but cannot easily convert firepower into political submission, and that dispersed missiles, hardened facilities, and prolonged conflict can strain American inventories and erode domestic consensus. China could apply those lessons in a confrontation over Taiwan.

Russia and North Korea are conducting similar assessments, but China has the greatest stake. Every month Washington remains heavily engaged in the Middle East is another month Beijing gains time to strengthen its own position in the Indo-Pacific. That should concern every American because China, not Iran, poses the greatest long-term challenge to American security and prosperity.

None of this argues for American retreat.

Quite the opposite.

President Trump now has an opportunity to restore strategic momentum by matching military power with a more clearly defined political strategy.

First, define a limited, achievable end state: deny Iran a nuclear-weapons capability, stop attacks on American forces and regional shipping, and make clear that renewed nuclear-weapons activity or attacks on U.S. interests trigger predictable consequences. Regime change should not be the unstated standard for victory.

Second, replace open-ended retaliation with clear deterrence. Washington should state plainly what triggers U.S. strikes, what would produce a pause, and what could open the door to negotiations.

Third, continue denying Iran access to its hardened nuclear infrastructure without committing large American ground forces. Rather than attempt an extraordinarily risky seizure of sites such as Pickaxe Mountain or Fordow, repeatedly deny access by collapsing entrances, cratering routes, maintaining surveillance, and striking renewed excavation.

Fourth, broaden the coalition. Keeping the Strait of Hormuz open should not remain primarily an American responsibility. Gulf partners, NATO allies, and other maritime nations share a vital interest in protecting Hormuz and should contribute more visibly. The burden, and the credibility, should be shared.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Finally, restore strategic focus. Iran is a dangerous regional power, but China remains America's principal long-term competitor. Washington must contain Tehran without letting the Middle East consume the resources and attention the Indo-Pacific requires.

American military power remains second to none. But bombs can destroy launchers, command centers, and tunnel entrances; they cannot alone compel a revolutionary regime to abandon its purpose.

President Trump’s task is not to bomb Iran until it becomes something it is not. It is to define an achievable objective, deny Tehran its most dangerous capabilities, share the burden with allies, and restore America’s strategic focus.

Military victories are remembered. History judges presidents by whether those victories produce political results, strengthen American credibility, and leave the nation safer.

item.title: New California law expands DNA tools for missing persons investigations
item.description: A new law signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom expands California's Missing Persons DNA Program to identify living and deceased victims across thousands of cold cases.
item.content:encoded:
A new California law is expanding the state’s use of DNA technology in missing persons investigations, giving authorities another tool to identify unknown people and revisit unresolved cases.

Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, signed the measure into law last month, loosening restrictions on California’s Missing Persons DNA Program.

The program had previously been limited to identifying deceased individuals. Under the expanded law, its database may also be used to identify unknown people who are alive, allowing state forensic resources to assist in a wider range of investigations.

MAN ACCUSED OF KILLING PARTNER ARRESTED IN MEXICO NEARLY TWO YEARS AFTER FLEEING WITH THEIR TWO CHILDREN

The program supports coroners, medical examiners and law enforcement agencies seeking to identify missing or unknown individuals across California.

"Any missing person case — adult, child, MMIP, or otherwise — is one too many. No family should know the prolonged uncertainty of waiting for answers, and together we’re making it clear that California takes action," state Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, said in a statement last month.

TEEN FOUND IN SHALLOW CALIFORNIA VINEYARD GRAVE IDENTIFIED NEARLY 50 YEARS LATER AS FAMILY WARNS KILLER

"AB 2018 is the right tool at the right time that will advance California’s ability to resolve missing persons cases and rekindle hope. I look forward to continuing the vital work of delivering justice for missing persons and their loved ones," he continued.

Assemblymember James Ramos, a Democrat, authored the legislation. He said the changes will make forensic identification resources more accessible to investigators and could help families who have waited years for answers.

"AB 2018 will help all families with missing loved ones receive the answers they need," Ramos said. "This modernization is especially urgent given the disproportionate number of missing and murdered Indigenous Persons plaguing our state. Ensuring our justice system personnel have the tools they need to perform effectively is critical to bringing resolution to cases involving the missing."

The law also changes how long certain DNA samples may remain in the state’s system.

Previously, DNA collected from relatives of missing people was destroyed after remains were identified. The state may now retain samples when investigators believe additional related remains could later be recovered and require identification.

The expanded authority comes as law enforcement agencies and forensic specialists in Northern California continue using newer DNA-analysis techniques to examine cold cases, according to Fox 40.

The Calaveras Cold Case Task Force was established in 2020 to reexamine unresolved cases in the county. The nonprofit team includes local law enforcement officials and scientists who use advanced forensic methods, including DNA analysis, to pursue new leads.

Supporters of the law say the changes could reduce barriers for local investigators while giving families of missing people a greater chance of learning what happened to their loved ones.

item.title: NASA opens first major new wind tunnel in more than 40 years at Virginia facility
item.description: NASA's new wind tunnel has a diameter of 20 feet and stands 24 feet tall, with wind speeds of up to 117 miles per hour. It will help test technology for future space missions.
item.content:encoded:
NASA opened its first major new wind tunnel in more than 40 years Friday, marking a milestone for future aviation and space-exploration research.

The Flight Dynamics Research Facility, located at the agency’s Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia, will serve as a testing ground for future aircraft and space missions.

"The opening of the Flight Dynamics Research Facility represents a significant advancement for NASA and for the nation," said Dr. Trina Dyal, NASA Langley center director. "By bringing modernized testing capabilities under one roof, we are enabling transformative research that will ensure the United States remains at the forefront of aeronautics and exploration."

NASA AT 68: AMERICA MUST LEAD ON THE MOON, MARS AND BEYOND — OR CHINA WILL

Built through a partnership with the U.S. General Services Administration, the more advanced and efficient tunnel replaces two facilities that had operated for more than 80 years.

NASA CHIEF CONFIRMS AGENCY HAS UNEXPLAINED UFO IMAGERY: 'WE DON'T KNOW WHAT IT IS'

The project is part of NASA’s broader effort to modernize its infrastructure and reduce the cost of maintaining aging facilities.

"If we continue to invest our resources, maintaining a lot of our historic facilities that have less current or anticipated demand," said Jared Isaacman, administrator of NASA, "it will come directly at the expense of the next generation capabilities that are going to be essential to again, meet the mission of today and also all that we imagine go forward."

NASA celebrated the facility’s opening with a ribbon-cutting ceremony at Langley attended by hundreds of industry leaders, government officials and community members. Some attendees later toured the new tunnel.

The 25,000-square-foot facility contains a vertical test section measuring 20 feet in diameter and 24 feet tall. The temperature-controlled tunnel can generate wind speeds of up to 117 mph.

NASA ADMINISTRATOR DETAILS MISSIONS TO MOON, MARS, VENUS AND THE AGENCY'S EFFORTS ON EARTH

"The capabilities in terms of wind speed that this can provide are much greater," said Giovanny Guecha, technical lead for the NASA Dragonfly parachute decelerator system. "It's almost a factor of ten compared to the previous way it's been done. So that helps us, you know, test more stressful conditions that are closer to Venus."

Four 750-horsepower motors power the tunnel, with each motor paired with a 14-foot-diameter, eight-bladed fan. The lightweight carbon-fiber blades allow engineers to adjust airflow quickly during free-flight testing and simulate flight at higher altitudes.

The wind tunnel will be used to test technology for future exploration of Venus and Titan, Saturn’s largest moon, as well as missions to Earth’s moon and Mars. It can also evaluate scale models of vehicles designed to travel through an atmosphere, including spacecraft returning to Earth.

"This facility will absolutely have a role in every future space mission," said David Storch, facility manager for NASA's transonic dynamics tunnel. "You know, anything that has to come back to Earth. Absolutely."

The facility will provide NASA and its partners with a critical resource for testing the safety and performance of future generations of aircraft, rockets, space-exploration vehicles, X-planes, drones and autonomous flight vehicles.

item.title: Todd Blanche moves closer to confirmation after rescinding $1.8B fund
item.description: Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche took a key step towards confirmation after meeting demands to rein in a settlement deal President Donald Trump reached with the IRS this year.
item.content:encoded:
Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche moved closer to Senate confirmation Sunday after formally rescinding a controversial $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization fund" and narrowing tax protections included in President Donald Trump’s IRS settlement.

A spokeswoman for Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, confirmed an agreement had been reached after Cornyn and Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., held up Blanche’s nomination. The agreement could clear the way for Cornyn to support Blanche at a Senate Judiciary Committee meeting Tuesday. Tillis had not publicly commented on the agreement as of Sunday night.

The committee is scheduled to vote on the nomination Tuesday, needing all Republicans on board to counter Democrats, who remain entirely opposed to Blanche's confirmation. An earlier committee vote was postponed after Cornyn and Tillis said they needed a written commitment from the administration.

Blanche formally met the senators’ demands by terminating the fund and clarifying that tax-related protections in the settlement apply only retroactively and do not cover future tax filings.

TRUMP BLASTS ROGUE GOP SENATORS FOR BLOCKING BLANCHE NOMINATION, VOWS ANTI-WEAPONIZATION BILL FIGHT

The fund never became operational: no members were appointed, no money was transferred, no claims process was established, and no payments were made, according to the Justice Department.

"My team and I have met with committee members and Senators over the past several weeks and addressed any concerns or outstanding questions," Blanche said in a post on X Sunday.

"We have enjoyed good faith discussions, and as a result issue the following order and update with regard to the May IRS settlement. The Department always welcomes and appreciates productive engagement with all members of Congress," he added.

Blanche’s order formally rescinded the May 18 directive establishing the fund and clarified that tax-related protections in the settlement apply only retroactively, not to future filings.

Cornyn and Tillis had sought the commitment in writing amid concerns that the fund could be revived, particularly as Trump continued to publicly support the idea. Lawmakers had also raised concerns that people convicted in connection with the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot could be eligible for payments.

"Sen. Cornyn has reached an agreement with the Department of Justice, which will be issuing a formal order permanently terminating the anti-weaponization fund and making clear in a binding written document that the scope of the audit settlement is limited to only the plaintiffs, including the President, and the IRS," Natalie Yezbick, a Cornyn spokesperson, told Politico.

Tillis had not announced whether the agreement was enough to secure his support.

Tillis is expected to follow Cornyn in backing Blanche on Tuesday after saying on Saturday, before the agreement was reached, that Trump "clearly intends to resurrect the payout pot for punks either by inappropriately establishing another bogus fund or pushing Congress to vote for a bill that the majority of Republicans in the Senate would be against."

TRUMP THREATENS TO YANK HIS OWN AG NOMINEE AS GOP REVOLT GROWS

"It’s unfortunate that Todd Blanche, who I consider qualified for the job, will not be confirmed because of this reversal. Hopefully, we can resolve this by Tuesday," Tillis said at the time.

Blanche has been serving as acting attorney general since he took over for Pam Bondi in April.

Senate Republicans hope to advance Blanche’s nomination before the end of the week.

item.title: Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski unloads on Angel Stadium mound after embarrassing Angels loss
item.description: Jacob Misiorowski called the Angel Stadium mound 'awful' after Wade Meckler's two-run homer lifted the Angels past the NL Central-leading Brewers.
item.content:encoded:
In a David-and-Goliath upset, the Angels stunned Jacob Misiorowski and the Brewers on Sunday afternoon, capping Milwaukee's three-day stay in Anaheim.

Afterward, Misiorowski said the mound at Angel Stadium was among the worst he'd ever pitched on.

"It was awful. It was probably one of the worst mounds I've had. It was dry; it was rock hard. I had the guys out there fix it three times, two times. And we got it back to being decent, but yeah, it was awful; it's bad," Misiorowski said (via Brewers beat writer Adam McCalvy).

REDS' DANE MYERS CARTED OFF FIELD AFTER CRASHING INTO WALL MAKING ACROBATIC CATCH VS BREWERS

Still, Miz made clear he wasn't using it as an excuse.

"It is what it is and you can't blame it on that. And I got to do my job."

Despite the defeat, Misiorowski still had a solid outing, allowing two runs on two hits over seven innings while striking out 10 and walking one.

ST. LOUIS CARDINALS VS. LOS ANGELES ANGELS BETTING PICK FAVORS THE HOME TEAM THROUGH FIVE INNINGS

The lone mistake was Wade Meckler's two-run homer in the second inning. His comments revived criticism of Angel Stadium's aging conditions, an issue many Angels fans have long associated with what they view as poor ownership.

Just this season, Angel Stadium closed an entire seating section because of a pest issue.

In the past, even players like Yusei Kikuchi have called out the aging infrastructure inside the stadium, citing the lack of basic major league amenities, including a broken air conditioner in the weight room.

PETE CROW-ARMSTRONG LAUNCHES SAVAGE EXTRA-INNING HOME RUN BEFORE CARDINALS GET THE LAST LAUGH

Misiorowski said the mound affected his outing, which was ultimately decided by Meckler's two-run homer.

Walbert Ureña, the Angels' starter who helped lead the shutout, did not offer similar complaints, prompting some fans to wonder whether Misiorowski's postgame comments were simply an excuse for an uncharacteristically rough outing.

On paper, the NL Central-leading Brewers looked like they should have cruised past the rebuilding Angels.

It wasn't all bad news for Milwaukee, which won Friday's and Saturday's games in Anaheim. On Saturday, the Angels abruptly scratched starting pitcher José Soriano, and the front office released an awkwardly timed statement explaining it was holding him out because of the possibility of a trade ahead of Monday's deadline.

Few teams have signaled they're sellers more aggressively than the Angels this season.

Baseball has a funny way of humbling its stars. Sunday was Misiorowski's turn.

item.title: Roman Reigns, Seth Rollins close important chapter of their history in colossal SummerSlam main event
item.description: Roman Reigns and Seth Rollins delivered an instant classic at SummerSlam, with spears, stomps and a steel chair callback to their Shield betrayal.
item.content:encoded:
Hatred. Brotherhood. Envy. Glory.

It’s those words that have described the relationship of Roman Reigns and Seth Rollins. The two entered WWE as members of The Shield and came into SummerSlam on Sunday night as enemies. Reigns put the World Heavyweight Championship on the line against Rollins for possibly the final time of their careers.

COMPLETE PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE ON FOX NEWS DIGITAL

Reigns and Rollins went blow-for-blow to start the match before it turned into an all-out brawl in the stands. Reigns delivered the first major blow to Rollins. He caught Rollins trying to spear him through the barricade and powerbombed him through an announce table.

Rollins struck back quickly and delivered his own powerbomb on Reigns through the other announce table. As the two rushed back into the ring, Rollins hit a pedigree on Reigns and tried to pick up the win there, but Reigns kicked out of the pin.

Rollins went back to the well and avoided a spear to hit a stomp. Still, he could not get the pin on Reigns.

The crowd at U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis watched closely as the two mammoth wrestling stars played a chess match to gain the smallest advantage. Rollins hit a superplex, but Reigns locked in a Kimura lock. Rollins, losing steam, stood back up and nearly hit a Falcon Arrow. Reigns slipped out and speared Rollins – one, two … so close.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Reigns resorted to smack talk, reminding Rollins that he'd always be No. 2 to him. But as Reigns bounced off the ropes, Rollins hit Reigns with a spear. Still, he couldn’t get the win.

In shades of WrestleMania, both men were putting on an instant classic in front of thousands of WWE fans. The two men, who know each other like the back of their hands. Reigns took a page out of Rollins’ playbook, hitting him with a buckle bomb and a stomp. Rollins got his arm up at the last possible second.

As the two went punch-for-punch, the referee went down. Reigns, in a nod to Dean Ambrose (now Jon Moxley), hit a Paradigm Shift. He went to spear Rollins, but Rollins pulled the referee in between them. It was anybody’s game now. Rollins looked at the title as he stepped over the carnage strewn across the outside ring area.

Rollins took a steel chair, which he used to betray Reigns 12 years ago. Reigns hit Rollins with a quick punch before Rollins could use the chair. Reigns looked at the chair. Rollins waited for Reigns to use the chair, but he cast it aside.

In a sign of mutual respect, Reigns demanded the two finish it in the middle of the ring without the weapon.

More stomps and spears from the two men without a referee kept the match going. The two former brothers locked eyes one last time. Reigns then delivered one last spear.

Reigns pinned Rollins to retain the World Heavyweight Championship.

For Reigns, it seems like the ghosts of his past have finally been dispelled. The two competitors looked at each other from the corner. Reigns put out his fist in a final Shield callback. Rollins obliged, leaving his Shield mask in the middle of the ring.

item.title: Deadliest animal in every US state revealed, from moose and bears to dogs
item.description: A new report identifies the deadliest animal in every U.S. state, with snakes leading nationwide while bears, sharks, insects and even dogs top other regions.
item.content:encoded:
A demographic data platform has released a new report identifying the animals most likely to kill people in each U.S. state.

The 2026 report from World Population Review revealed a surprising mix of creatures topping the list, from large mammals such as moose to unexpected threats such as dogs and jellyfish.

According to the report, snakes make up the single largest category nationwide, with several species of rattlesnakes topping the list in multiple regions.

Georgia residents should be most cautious of the pygmy rattlesnake, while Oklahoma's biggest snake threat is the western pygmy rattlesnake.

CALIFORNIA TODDLER BITTEN BY RATTLESNAKE HIDING BENEATH AMAZON PACKAGE AMID ACTIVE SNAKE SEASON

Meanwhile, Timber rattlesnakes claimed the top spot in both Connecticut and Kansas.

Southern Pacific rattlesnakes pose the biggest threat in California, while Arizona's deadliest species is the western diamondback rattlesnake.

Other rattlesnakes dominating state hazards include the prairie rattlesnake in North Dakota, the Mojave rattlesnake in Nevada and the eastern massasauga in Michigan.

Several non-rattlesnake species also rank as the deadliest animals in their respective states.

Louisiana's top threat is the eastern diamondback rattlesnake and Mississippi's is the cottonmouth snake.

Similarly, Indiana leads with the eastern copperhead, South Carolina points to the southern copperhead, and Hawaii stands out with the yellow-bellied sea snake as its primary concern.

NO CURE, NO VACCINE: EXPERTS WARN OF RARE BOURBON VIRUS AFTER FIRST NY CASE

Beyond reptiles, several states face risks from insects and other venomous creatures. 

Wasps top the list in Iowa, ticks take the lead in Missouri, mosquitoes pose the highest danger in New York, and black widow spiders are the main concern in Alabama and Nebraska.

A handful of states should be cautious around coastal waters, according to the report.

Tiger sharks rank as the deadliest animal in Rhode Island, while bull sharks pose the greatest threat in Maryland and Virginia.

A jellyfish-like marine creature, called the Portuguese man o' war, is listed as the biggest danger in Delaware and North Carolina. Experts say that while its sting can be deadly in rare cases, it more commonly causes painful welts and skin irritation.

Alligators also rank as the deadliest animal in Florida and Texas, with the American alligator specifically topping Florida's list.

Large mammals also appear prominently throughout the report, with black bears ranking as the deadliest animals in Tennessee and Wisconsin.

North American black bears pose the greatest threat in Oregon, while American black bears top the list in Kentucky and Massachusetts.

In contrast, New Mexico's deadliest animal is the mountain lion, while moose are listed as the greatest risk in Colorado, Maine, New Hampshire and Vermont.

Grizzly bears also top the list in Idaho, Montana and Washington, and bison pose the greatest danger in South Dakota and Wyoming.

Whitetail deer were also identified as the deadliest animals in Arkansas, Ohio, West Virginia and Pennsylvania.

In Alaska, despite commonly being household pets, dogs are listed as the state's most concerning animal.

Similarly, coyotes rank as the biggest threat in Illinois, Minnesota, New Jersey and Utah.

Overall, snakes dominate the threat landscape, topping the list in 14 states, according to the report.

Bears threaten eight states, while deer and other large ungulates account for 10 states.

Canines, including dogs and coyotes, rank as the deadliest animals in five states.

Biting and stinging arthropods, such as wasps, mosquitos and spiders, account for five states.

Equally, marine hazards also account for five states.

item.title: Gavin Williams' perfect game bid leads to benches-clearing altercation between Guardians and Diamondbacks
item.description: Gavin Williams was pitching a perfect game before Tim Tawa's controversial bunt attempt sparked a benches-clearing scrum during a rain delay.
item.content:encoded:
The Cleveland Guardians went from watching starter Gavin Williams go from pitching a perfect game to a benches-clearing altercation in the matter of moments at Progressive Field on Sunday.

Williams was humming to start this contest, striking out 10 of the first 15 hitters he faced, and as the top of the sixth began, he was looking at a perfect game bid.

But things got interesting when Arizona Diamondbacks center fielder Tim Tawa attempted a bunt on a 0-1 pitch from Williams in the frame. In the unwritten rules of baseball, bunting while a pitcher is throwing a perfect game is very much frowned upon.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Guardians catcher Patrick Bailey took exception, having words with Tawa before the right-handed hitter stepped back in the box.

In the end, though, Tawa served a single to right field and ended both the perfect game and no-hit bid for Williams.

CINCINNATI REDS PITCHER RIPS 'F—ING FATA–' UMPIRE FOR GETTING IN DEFENDER'S WAY ON GROUND BALL

Just a few pitches later, rain in the Cleveland area started coming down in buckets. After Williams threw a brutal wild pitch, umpires called a rain delay, as the grounds crew came sprinting out with the tarp.

But as the tarp was still unfurling, both dugouts were on the field and near home plate as an argument broke out. Guardians manager Stephen Vogt was seen walking out of the dugout with pace to clearly say something to the other side, and that sparked the scrum near the dish.

While it was clear both teams were screaming some unkind words toward each other, nothing escalated into a physical altercation between the two teams. It can be implied that Vogt took exception to Tawa’s bunt attempt, but it’s unknown what he said exactly toward the D-Backs.

Then again, the other side of the argument is any hitter can attempt to reach base how they see fit. If it’s a 450-foot home run, or a bunt single, that’s the batter’s right.

But when the Guardians were facing the Minnesota Twins on July 9, Williams was also in a perfect game scenario when Royce Lewis showed bunt during an at-bat. He would eventually hit a single like Tawa did to end the bid.

When the rain delay finally ended, and both teams cooled the tension, the Guardians continued to dominate with a 5-0 victory at home. The Diamondbacks were only able to muster one hit after Tawa’s single, while the Guardians tallied eight hits on the day.

Rookie Chase DeLauter went 2-for-4 with three RBI, while Bailey crushed a home run in his 1-for-3 day at the plate.

Williams never made it back into the game after the rain delay, finishing his day with 5.2 innings pitched, 10 strikeouts, one hit and one walk allowed.

item.title: Saints make shocking Ja'Lynn Polk retirement move after former second-round pick disappears
item.description: Ja'Lynn Polk scrubbed his Instagram and went dark just days before the Saints placed the 24-year-old wide receiver on the reserve/retired list.
item.content:encoded:
At 24 years old, most NFL wideouts are chasing their first major payday. Ja'Lynn Polk is calling it quits. The New Orleans Saints stunned the NFL on Sunday by placing the former second-round pick on the reserve/retired list.

Days before the retirement announcement, Kellen Moore revealed Polk had been away from the team for personal reasons, offering few details.

Shortly after, Polk scrubbed his Instagram account clean and went dark. Less than three years after helping Washington play for a national championship, Polk is stepping away from the NFL.

CARDINALS TIGHT END TRAVIS VOKOLEK RETIRES AT AGE 28 AFTER SUFFERING SEVERE NECK INJURY DURING 2025 SEASON

Polk's pro career never gained traction. He caught 12 passes for 87 yards and two touchdowns during a difficult rookie season in New England.

Despite the disappointing debut, Polk insisted he never lost confidence, telling reporters before the 2025 season, "I don't even think about last year," while adding that he still believed he was "going to be great."

A shoulder injury then wiped out his entire 2025 season, prompting the Patriots to send him to New Orleans in a late-round pick swap while he was still on injured reserve.

DETROIT LIONS GREAT FRANK RAGNOW DETAILS HIS ABRUPT RETIREMENT, FAILED COMEBACK ATTEMPT

After spending nearly a full year rehabbing his shoulder, Polk walked away without playing a regular-season snap for the Saints.

Polk has not publicly explained his decision.

The Saints retain his rights if he ever decides to return, but for now, a career that began with second-round expectations has ended after just two seasons.

item.title: Trailblazing former Republican Rep Kay Granger dies at 83: 'Broke barriers'
item.description: Former Rep. Kay Granger, a trailblazing Texas Republican who served nearly three decades in Congress and became Fort Worth’s first female mayor, has died at 83.
item.content:encoded:
Former Rep. Kay Granger, R-Texas, died on Sunday at the age of 83, with her ex-colleagues remembering her as a trailblazer who broke barriers for women.

Granger was the first woman elected mayor of Fort Worth, Texas, as well as the first Republican woman from the Lone Star State elected to the U.S. House of Representatives and the first female Republican appropriations chair.

After serving in the U.S. House from 1997, Granger retired in January of last year following health challenges and extended absences from Washington.

"As many of my family, friends, and colleagues have known, I have been navigating some unforeseen health challenges over the past year," she said in December 2024. "However, since early September, my health challenges have progressed, making frequent travel to Washington both difficult and unpredictable. During this time, my incredible staff has remained steadfast, continuing to deliver exceptional constituent services, as they have for the past 27 years."

SEN BERNIE MORENO CALLS FOR EX-SON-IN-LAW TO RESIGN FROM HOUSE, GET 'SERIOUS PSYCHOLOGICAL HELP'

Republican and Democratic lawmakers said they remember Granger as someone who broke barriers for women.

"Kay Granger devoted her life to serving her Fort Worth, Texas community — as a teacher and businesswoman, on the Fort Worth Zoning Commission and City Council, as Mayor, and in Congress for nearly three decades, where she also served as Chairwoman of the House Appropriations Committee. Throughout her career, she broke barriers for women in public service," House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said in a statement.

"Kelly and I send our prayers to her family, loved ones, and the Fort Worth community as we remember her extraordinary life of service and lasting legacy. She was a dear friend who will be greatly missed," he added.

Rep. Lisa McClain, R-Mich., who serves as chair of the House Republican Caucus, said Granger "was a pioneer, a dedicated public servant, and a trailblazing leader who opened doors for generations of Republican women to follow."

"Her impact on Congress and our Nation will not be forgotten. My prayers are with her family and loved ones. Rest in peace," McClain said.

House Appropriations Committee Ranking Member Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., said she was "deeply saddened" by her passing, saying the former GOP lawmaker "devoted her life to serving the people of Texas and our nation with integrity, determination, and a profound sense of duty."

DEMOCRATS TARGET MORE GOP HOUSE SEATS AFTER SOCIALIST VICTORIES ROCK LEFT-WING PRIMARIES

"Throughout our years serving together on the Appropriations Committee, we worked through difficult challenges with mutual respect and honesty," DeLauro said. "Congresswoman Granger was the first woman to sit on and serve as chair of the Defense Appropriations Subcommittee. She was the first Republican woman to lead the full Appropriations Committee, and with our counterparts Senators Patty Murray and Susan Collins, was part of the first Committee led on all four corners by women."

"At every step of her career, she earned the respect of Members on both sides of the aisle through her steady leadership and deep belief in the importance of Congress fulfilling its constitutional responsibility to invest in the American people," DeLauro added.

item.title: Donald Trump's granddaughter Kai Trump reveals her unexpected song of the year pick

Absolutely, completely, utterly correct. CNN, Bash, Tapper, all of them, unquestioningly believed everything Anthony Fauci said, because they have the same political views. That's it.
